methodological_questions: How to operationally define a failed PNR possession?
How reliable is the classification of pull-up shots from play-by-play data?
What is the appropriate baseline for computing lift of pull-up as a counter?
What unit of analysis provides sufficient sample size while meeting the >70% criterion?
How to control for confounding by shot-clock, game situation, and shot difficulty?

historical_evidence.finding: Play-type classifier assisted-flag leak: assisted flag exists only on makes, causing SPOT_UP 2.83 PPP (100% makes). After rewrite, SPOT_UP ~1.16 PPP. This artifact can infect any possession-level play type inference that uses the assisted flag.
2024-25 shot-level PNR share of half-court shots varies by team (7.6–13.8%). Possession-level PNR rates are higher (~17.9–19.6% later calibrated).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Play-type classification using the NBA assisted flag
failed_approaches.why: The assisted flag is recorded only on made field goals, leading to severe upward bias in PPP for play types that depend on it (e.g., SPOT_UP reached 2.83 PPP). The underlying classification logic is fragile and may affect PULL_UP labeling as well.

evidence_establishes: A known data artifact in play-type classification inflates PPP when the assisted flag is used; a corrected version exists but must be verified for PULL_UP.
Shot-level PNR identification from play-by-play is feasible and yields team-level rates that align with later possession-level calibrations.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether PULL_UP classification is accurate after the artifact fix.
How PNR fail can be reliably identified from the graph database possessions.
Any direct empirical evidence on the effectiveness of pull-up shots as a counter after PNR failure.
What a reasonable baseline for lift should be and how large unit-level samples would be.
own_inferences: The requirement that ≥70% of units show lift > 0 with a median lift > 2 pp is an unusually strong claim; prior work on exploitable defensive weaknesses (FAM:SF-APPA-034) found edges available only 33% of the time and median best edge ~3.79%, suggesting that broadly distributed genuine lift is rare.
The unit of analysis is crucial: player-level units will suffer from small samples; team-offense units (n≈30) would have moderate samples but make the binomial threshold coarse and power low.
Any pull‑up after a PNR fail is likely to occur under non-optimal conditions (late clock, defensive pressure), making it difficult to disentangle the counter effect from situational suppression.
uncertainties: The exact operational definition of PNR fail (e.g., turnover, scoreless possession, or PPP below a threshold) is unspecified.
It is unknown whether the play-type possession records used by the graph database have been fully updated to remove the assisted‑flag artifact.
The typical number of pull‑up shots following PNR fail per team‑season is unknown and could be too low for reliable measurement.
Potential confounding by shot difficulty, shot clock, and score margin has not been explored in this context.

historical_effect.explanation: The discovery of the assisted-flag artifact (FAM:SF-PAP-096) introduces a critical data-quality risk that was not anticipated in the original question; it forces a validation step before any analysis. Additionally, prior prevalence work (FAM:SF-APPA-034) shifts the prior toward low probability of finding widespread genuine lift, making the 70%/2pp threshold less plausible.

blocking_constraints.text: Possession-level labeling of PNR fail and PULL_UP from play-by-play may be unreliable: the previously observed assisted-flag artifact could still bias pull‑up PPP, and PNR fail identification has not been validated.
The number of possessions that match the sequence (PNR fail → pull‑up) could be very small per unit, making individual lift estimates too noisy to support the 70% threshold.

Pull‑up shots taken after a failed PNR are likely to occur later in the shot clock and under greater defensive pressure, confounding the effect of the counter strategy with normal situational suppression.
Historical evidence suggests that genuine defensive edges that produce consistently positive lift across many units are rare; the prior probability of meeting the stated thresholds is low.

prior_work.summary: No earlier work directly tested the PNR-fail→pull‑up counter hypothesis. The most relevant findings are a know artifact in play-type classification (FAM:SF-PAP-096) and descriptive evidence on PNR rates (FAM:SF-APPM-058). Another study (FAM:SF-APPA-034) showed that opponent‑specific exploitable edges exist only 33% of the time and median best edge is about 3.79%, suggesting that widespread genuine lift of 2 pp is uncommon.

risks.text: Possession-level play‑type labels (PNR, PULL_UP) from the graph database may still be contaminated by the assisted‑flag artifact or have high misclassification rates.
Many potential units of analysis (e.g., player‑pairings) will have extremely few PNR‑fail→pull‑up observations, yielding unstable and overfit lift estimates.
Game situation (shot clock, score margin, defensive pressure) is a strong confounder: pull‑ups after PNR fails may systematically differ in difficulty from other pull‑ups, biasing lift.
Even if a single joint inference is planned, exploration across units and definitions can inflate false positive risk if not pre‑registered.
The low prior probability of real strategic edges being both positive and large weakens the evidential value of the proposed thresholds.

design.estimand: For each unit (team‑offense, over a multi‑season window), the difference in points per possession on pull‑up shots that follow a failed PNR possession versus pull‑up shots that follow a non‑failed PNR or other half‑court possessions, adjusted for shot distance and shot‑clock remaining.
design.sample: All regular‑season games from the 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26 seasons, using per‑game play‑by‑play and the derived possession graph after the artifact fix (confirmed no assisted‑flag leak on pull‑ups).
design.power: Assuming each team has ~800 total pull‑up shots over 4 seasons and ~20% occur after a PNR fail, there would be ~160 pull‑ups per team; a 2 pp lift (σ≈1.2 pp per shot) would have moderate power (~0.6) at α=0.05 per team, but the joint binomial‑median test has limited power with only 30 units.
design.controls: Shot distance (binned), shot‑clock remaining (linear and squared), game score margin, home/away indicator, and opponent defensive rating (or team‑fixed effects).
design.falsification: Before analysis, compute overall PPP on all pull‑up shots; if it exceeds 1.20 PPP or is suspiciously correlated with assisted rate, the play‑type classification is deemed unreliable and the study is halted. Also check that PNR‑fail rate is not trivially correlated with team pace.
design.multiplicity: A single pre‑registered global test: binomial test H0: P(lift>0) ≤ 0.7 vs. H1: >0.7, and median lift > 0.02 PPP (using bootstrap). No per‑unit tests are conducted, so multiplicity is controlled.
design.decision_rule: If 21 or more teams (70% of 30) have estimated lift > 0 and the median lift exceeds 0.02 PPP, the hypothesis is considered supported; otherwise it is rejected or declared insufficient evidence (depending on the estimated uncertainty).
design.data_version: Data as of 2026-05-23, with play‑type possession records rebuilt after the FAM:SF-PAP-096 artifact correction. The analysis must be preceded by a thorough validation that the pull‑up classification does not suffer from the assisted‑flag bias.
